title: mattpocock/skills — grilling/SKILL.md (the actual grill-me interview engine)
snippet: The model-invoked engine behind grill-me. Defines a design-tree / frontier / round protocol for interviewing a user about a plan or design before acting.
quote: Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. [...] The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

credibility.note: primary source, verbatim fetch of the named target.

title: Clarify When Necessary: Resolving Ambiguity Through Interaction with LMs (Zhang & Choi, NAACL Findings 2025)
snippet: Task-agnostic framework for evaluating a system's ability to decide WHEN to ask for clarification, across QA/MT/NLI, using an entropy-over-user-intents estimator (INTENT-SIM).
quote: Determining when to ask for clarification is a challenging task that requires systems to consider the demands of the individual user (i.e., how much they prioritize speed and usability versus carefulness) and the distribution of interpretations for a given request (i.e., whether an ambiguous request has one dominant, inferable interpretation).

credibility.note: peer-reviewed NAACL Findings 2025 paper, ACL Anthology. High tier, directly on-topic for ask-vs-act policy design, but scoped to single-turn conversational QA/MT/NLI, not agent execution.

title: Knowing When to Ask: Self-Gated Clarification for Hierarchical Language Agents (Gao, Kang, Wang, Woo — AWS)
snippet: Places clarification INSIDE the agent's action space on the same ordinal scale as navigation actions ('ActionRating'), so asking competes directly with acting at every decision point, distinguishing mandatory (no viable branch) vs opportunistic (residual uncertainty despite a leading candidate) clarification.
quote: Rather than treating clarification as an external uncertainty trigger, we propose ActionRating, a formulation that places it inside the agent's action space on a shared ordinal scale with navigation, so that asking competes directly with acting at every decision point and help-seeking becomes observable at intermediate states.

credibility.note: arXiv preprint, industry lab (AWS), evaluated on a 30k-node taxonomy classification benchmark — a hierarchical-decision setting, not free-form coding-agent execution. Directly relevant mechanism (asking-as-an-action) but domain differs materially from ours.

title: Knowing but Not Showing: LLMs Recognize Ambiguity but Rarely Ask Clarifying Questions (Su & Cardie)
snippet: Finding that LLMs often internally represent/recognize an ambiguous request but default to answering directly rather than asking — a gap between latent recognition and surfaced behavior.
quote: LLMs Recognize Ambiguity but Rarely Ask Clarifying Questions

credibility.note: arXiv preprint (2026-05-24), 0 citations at retrieval — very recent, unreplicated. Title/topic-level citation only; full text not crawled in this pass.

title: Act or Clarify? Modeling Sensitivity to Uncertainty and Cost in Communication (Tsvilodub & Mulligan, Tübingen)
snippet: Computational/linguistic model of when a rational communicator should act on an ambiguous instruction vs. ask, trading off uncertainty against the cost of asking.
quote: Act or Clarify? Modeling Sensitivity to Uncertainty and Cost in Communication

credibility.note: arXiv preprint, linguistics/cognitive-science framing. Title-level citation; models a COST of asking explicitly, which is the closest literature analog to our 'interruption cost' concern, but in a conversational (not mid-execution) setting.

title: CLAM: Selective Clarification for Ambiguous Questions with Generative Language Models (Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar)
snippet: Introduces selective clarification: a system that detects when its own answer would likely be wrong due to ambiguity and asks instead of guessing.
quote: Users often ask dialogue systems ambiguous questions that require clarification. We show that current language models rarely ask users to clarify ambiguous questions and instead provide incorrect answers.

credibility.note: peer-adjacent arXiv preprint from an established uncertainty-estimation lab (Kuhn/Gal/Farquhar — semantic entropy). Single-turn QA setting, pre-task.

title: CLAMBER: A Benchmark of Identifying and Clarifying Ambiguous Information Needs in LLMs (ACL 2024)
snippet: Benchmark for whether a system correctly identifies WHEN a query is ambiguous enough to need clarification, prior to any task execution.
quote: CLAMBER: A Benchmark of Identifying and Clarifying Ambiguous Information Needs in Large Language Models

credibility.note: peer-reviewed ACL 2024 long paper. Pre-task, information-need framing — intake-time, not mid-execution.

title: Agent Loop Detection: Definition & FutureAGI Guide (2026)
snippet: Vendor glossary entry distinguishing an obvious infinite-loop failure from a quieter 'stalled loop' failure where every step is syntactically valid but no step advances the task.
quote: The quieter failure is a stalled loop, where every step is syntactically valid but no step moves the task closer to completion.

credibility.note: vendor content marketing (FutureAGI, an agent-observability company) — commercial bias toward selling observability tooling; useful vocabulary, not independently verified research.

title: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents (Hou, Wang, Zhao, Wang — HUST)
snippet: Defines Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs) as a structural class of failure in agent frameworks (unbounded feedback paths across LLM calls, tool invocations, agent handoffs) and builds IAL-Scan, a static analyzer over an Agent IR / Agentic Loop Dependence Graph, validated on 6,549 real agent repos (74 findings, 91.9% precision on 68 confirmed).
quote: We define an IAL as an execution failure in which an agentic feedback path repeatedly triggers LLM calls, tool invocations, agent executions, or workflow transitions without an effective termination condition.

credibility.note: arXiv preprint, academic (HUST), large-scale empirical validation (6,549 repos). Static-analysis / code-structure framing — detects a STRUCTURAL absence of a bound, not a semantic/content thrash like ours (repeated review findings). Distinguishing this from our target is itself a finding.

title: Loop drift: how agents convince themselves they're making progress (Loop & Retry blog, 2026-07-07)
snippet: Practitioner teardown of a real 41-step agent run that burned 15x normal tokens narrating false progress; argues a step cap is a backstop not a detector, and that asking the model to self-assess progress fails because 'the model's sense of progress is generated from the same context that's drifting.'
quote: We trusted the model's self-assessment. This is the deep one. Our loop asked the model, each step, whether it was making progress and whether it was done — and the model said yes, it was progressing, right up to the cap. [...] The model's sense of progress is generated from the same context that's drifting. Every 'I'm narrowing it down' was a fluent continuation of a transcript full of fluent continuations. A drifting agent's self-report drifts with it. Asking a stuck agent whether it's stuck is asking the unreliable narrator to review their own reliability.

credibility.note: practitioner blog, single incident teardown, no peer review, author/org identity not fully verifiable. Directly on-point analytic claim (self-report is an unreliable detector) but evidence is anecdotal (n=1 case study).

title: kneelinghorse/agent-vitals — health monitor for production AI agents
snippet: OSS Python library computing loop/stuck/thrash/runaway-cost detection from 4 per-step signals (findings_count, coverage_score, total_tokens, error_count); framework adapters for LangChain/LangGraph/CrewAI/AutoGen/DSPy/Haystack/Langfuse/LangSmith; ships a backtest harness with P/R/F1 metrics against recorded trajectories.
quote: **The direct-integration health monitor for production AI agents** — detect loops, stuck states, confabulation, thrash, and runaway costs with four numbers per step.

credibility.note: OSS project, 0 GitHub stars at retrieval — unvalidated by community adoption. Its 4-signal design (progress/coverage/cost/error) is architecturally the closest analog found to a mid-execution 'residue' detector, and it explicitly names 'thrash' as a target class.

title: synthet1cc/unloop-mcp — MCP server that detects AI fix loops and forces course correction
snippet: Fingerprints each error (stripping paths/line numbers/timestamps) and compares fix-attempt descriptions via Jaccard similarity; flags a loop above a 55% similarity threshold; three escalation levels (NUDGE at 3-4 attempts, WARNING at 5-6, CRITICAL at 7+ — 'STOP. Revert everything. Ask the user for help.').
quote: **2. Unloop Detects the Loop** — The engine normalizes each error into a fingerprint (stripping paths, line numbers, timestamps) and compares fix descriptions using Jaccard similarity. When similarity exceeds 55%, it flags a loop. [...] | **CRITICAL** | 7+ attempts | "STOP. Revert everything. Ask the user for help." |

credibility.note: OSS project, small (4 stars, 8 open issues) — unvalidated at scale, thresholds (55% similarity, attempt counts) appear tuned by author intuition not measured against ground truth. Nonetheless the single closest prior-art match found for 'detect thrash from residue, escalate, eventually ask the operator' — same shape as yf-judgement's target behavior, but scoped to single-error fix loops, not cross-review-pass semantic recurrence.

title: Yingqi-Han/learning-retrospective-skill — breaking retry loops, capturing verified lessons
snippet: Distinguishes known problems (a stored lesson covers the failure signature — recall and follow it) from novel problems (explore freely, never retry verbatim, capture the lesson after solving); detects exact retry candidates and escalates short activity/failure windows to a bounded semantic reviewer; hooks into harness failure-detection events.
quote: Failure is not error — repeated attempts on a novel problem are legitimate exploration. The waste this skill targets is solving the **same** problem twice: struggling through a failure loop that a past session already resolved, because the lesson was never captured or never recalled.

credibility.note: OSS project, small (2 stars). Notable for explicitly separating legitimate iteration from wasteful repetition — directly relevant to our false-positive-cost question (Q secondary 2) — but its ground truth is 'a lesson was already captured,' a form of evidence our mid-execution setting does not have on a first occurrence.

title: Towards a typology of questions for requirements elicitation interviews (Zaremba & Liaskos, IEEE RE 2021)
snippet: Cross-disciplinary (software engineering, psychology, sociology, knowledge management, library science, journalism, health care, judicial investigation) literature review building a typology of interview-question dimensions: content, style/probing-style, sequence, objective. Cites Derr's Aristotelian/Kantian question-content categories (existence, identity, properties, relations, number, time, location, action) and Burnay et al.'s Elicitation Topic Map (6 topic sets: items, rules, localization / activities, connections, granularity; ~30 topics).
quote: Content is concerned with what the interviewer is interested in finding out about when asking a question. [...] R. Derr [4], inspired by the philosophical work of Aristotle and Kant, characterize question content based on the concept that the question presupposes. Thus, in reference to an object [...] one can question its existence, its identity, its properties, its relations to other objects, the number of the objects, if they are many, its time and location as well as whether the object is performing an action.

credibility.note: peer-reviewed IEEE RE 2021 conference paper, explicitly a cross-disciplinary literature synthesis (its stated method). Highest-tier source in this cluster for the requirements-engineering question-taxonomy sub-question. Pre-task interview setting — the interviewee is a live human being interviewed synchronously, not residue being read after the fact.

title: Ordering interrogative questions for effective requirements engineering: The W6H pattern (Sultan & Miranskyy, RePa 2015)
snippet: Proposes ordering interview questions using a Who/What/When/Where/Why/hoW (W6H) interrogative pattern to maximize elicitation accuracy.
quote: Ordering interrogative questions for effective requirements engineering: The W6H pattern

credibility.note: peer-reviewed IEEE workshop paper (RePa 2015). Title/topic-level citation; a concrete, portable question-slotting scheme (W6H) that is domain-agnostic enough it plausibly transfers past the conversational setting — worth follow-up if the design phase wants a ready-made ontology.

title: Ambiguity and tacit knowledge in requirements elicitation interviews (Ferrari, Spoletini, Gnesi, RE 2015 journal version)
snippet: Studies how ambiguity in customer-analyst communication during elicitation interviews is a major obstacle to knowledge transfer, and how tacit knowledge underlies much of that ambiguity.
quote: Ambiguity in communication is often perceived as a major obstacle for knowledge transfer, which could...

credibility.note: peer-reviewed (Requirements Engineering journal, Springer). Establishes that ambiguity in RE is bound up with TACIT knowledge the speaker doesn't know they're withholding — relevant to why a question needs to surface an assumption, not just request more words.

title: otar/clarify-skill — Claude Code plugin, interrogates a request before any work starts
snippet: User-invoked /clarify skill using the AskUserQuestion tool (2-4 clickable options each, recommended default up front); explicitly framed as pre-task ('before any work starts') and manually invoked only (disable-model-invocation:true, matching grill-me's pattern).
quote: It interrogates your request with structured, clickable questions until it's unambiguous, before any work starts. [...] The skill leans toward asking — it surfaces borderline ambiguity rather than guessing.

credibility.note: OSS project, 0 stars. Another pre-task-only design (same class as grill-me/socrates) confirming the pattern: publicly discoverable 'ask before acting' skills cluster at intake, none found scoped to mid-execution.

title: What Makes Interruptions Disruptive? (Borst, Taatgen, van Rijn, CHI 2015)
snippet: Computational cognitive model of task interruption/resumption based on the 'problem state bottleneck': disruptiveness driven by interruption duration, interrupting-task complexity, and moment of interruption; problem-state requirements of BOTH tasks predict disruption.
quote: The experiments confirmed that problem state requirements are an important predictor for the disruptiveness of interruptions. This suggests that interfaces should be designed to a) interrupt users at low-problem state moments and b) maintain the problem state for the user when interrupted.

credibility.note: peer-reviewed CHI 2015 paper, cognitive-science methodology. The clearest HCI grounding found for 'the cost of asking is an interruption, not a conversational turn' — but it models interrupting a HUMAN's task, not the cost of an autonomous agent run pausing itself; the transfer direction is inverted from ours (we interrupt the operator's attention, not the agent's task state) and needs explicit translation.

title: If Not Now, When?: The Effects of Interruption at Different Moments Within Task Execution (Adamczyk & Bailey, CHI 2004)
snippet: Foundational HCI study measuring the effect of interruption TIMING (moment within a task's execution) on performance, emotional state, and social attribution toward the interrupting system, using task models from event-perception research to predict cognitive load at each moment.
quote: Our results show that different interruption moments have different impacts on user emotional state and positive social attribution, and suggest that a system could enable a user to maintain a high level of awareness while mitigating the disruptive effects of interruption.

credibility.note: peer-reviewed, highly-cited foundational CHI 2004 paper; the interruptions.net literature archive is a specialist archive (Bailey lab) — high credibility. Establishes 'boundary moments' (breakpoints between subtasks) as lower-cost interruption points, a concept that DOES plausibly transfer: a review-pass boundary or a bead-close event is a candidate low-cost interruption point in our setting.
